newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss reject labour law, political asylum changes.
newsitem.headline: Swiss reject labour law, political asylum changes.

text.p: Swiss voters taking part in two referendums on Sunday firmly rejected proposals to liberalise labour laws, but only narrowly threw out a far-right initiative to restrict political asylum rights.

Final counts in the country's 26 cantons showed 67 percent rejected the labour law revision, which would have opened the way for more overtime and lifted a ban on Swiss women working night shifts in factories.
The pro-business FDP party had favoured the bill, which was seen as a way to help the country's flagging economy, but opponents believed that it was too heavily weighted in favour of employers.
In a much closer vote on the asylum issue, the final count according to official government figures showed 53.7 percent of voters against the measure.
The bill, which was supported by the rightist Swiss People's Party (SVP), would have barred foreigners deemed to have entered the country illegally from seeking asylum.
Meanwhile, in a controversial regional referendum, Zurich voters came out in favour of continuing a programme that provides heroin for addicts.
Swiss radio said 62 percent of voters supported a continuation of the pilot programme, which requires funding of 4.7 million Swiss francs ($3.61 million).

Zurish tolerated drugs in controlled areas for a while in the 1990s, earning one area the name "needle park." But the city's efforts to control its drug problem appeared to attract addicts from across Europe.

In remarks welcoming the rejection of labour law changes, spokeswoman Ursula Cridazzi of the Confederation of Swiss Employees Association, representing Swiss trade unions of white collar employees in the private sector, said:
"We are very glad that it was rejected, because we count on having a better revision in the law, which will give more protection to working people, and not only deregulation."

The far-right Swiss Democrats (SD) party said in a statement it regretted the failure of the asylum bill, but noted how close it came to passing, saying this showed how split the mood was in the country.
"Once more, it has been demonstrated that our population is split into two relatively compact blocs with respect to the immigration question," the SD said in a statement.
"The vote-struggle reveals a great dissatisfaction of many people." it said. ($1=1.3007 Swiss Franc)
